title: Blood Tests Reveal Why Astronauts Get Constipated in Space
summary:
Constipation is a common complaint for astronauts, but until now, scientists didn't fully understand why. New research from the University of Copenhagen, done with NASA, offers a possible answer — and it starts with your gut bacteria.

Researchers analyzed blood samples from 52 astronauts who spent months aboard the International Space Station. They found signs that the digestive system begins changing relatively soon after astronauts leave Earth. Specifically, gut bacteria start fermenting protein more than usual.

Normally, bacteria in the intestines break down fiber from food. But when fiber runs out, they switch to protein. That process — protein fermentation — isn't unique to space; it happens on Earth too. The difference is that in space, it seems to happen more.

'We see changes in astronauts' blood samples that indicate that the gut bacteria begin to ferment protein to a greater extent than usual within weeks after the astronauts arrive in space, and this change continues until they are back on Earth,' says Giorgia La Barbera, joint first author and associate professor at the University of Copenhagen.

The researchers suspect that microgravity slows the movement of food through the digestive tract. If food stays in the intestines longer, bacteria have more time to turn to protein fermentation. 'The lack of gravity in space probably causes food to move more slowly through the intestine, and this fits with the fact that we are seeing signs of increased protein fermentation,' says co-author Henrik Roager. 'This may also help explain constipation in astronauts.'

The findings came from analyzing metabolites — small molecules in the blood that reveal how the body is working. The results could matter beyond digestion because gut changes can affect other parts of the body, including the brain. 'We know that products of protein fermentation [are] often associated with negative health consequences, such as kidney damage, potential effects on mood or reduced ability to focus,' says senior author Lars Ove Dragsted.

Why does this matter? Because space agencies are planning longer missions to the Moon and eventually Mars. Astronauts on those journeys would spend far more time away from Earth's gravity. The team suggests possible fixes: more dietary fiber, prebiotics, or treatments that promote peristalsis — the muscle contractions that move food and waste through the digestive system. These could help astronauts — and maybe people on Earth with similar gut problems.
why_it_matters: As space agencies plan long missions to the Moon and eventually Mars, small digestive problems could become mission-threatening health risks, and the same gut science may end up helping people on Earth with similar digestive conditions.

background_read: NASA (the United States' space agency) and other space agencies have studied how spaceflight affects the human body for decades; crews on the International Space Station (a football-field-sized laboratory orbiting Earth, continuously occupied since 2000) lose bone density and muscle mass, and their hearts and eyes change too.

The gut microbiome — the trillions of bacteria living in the human intestine — helps digest food, make vitamins and train the immune system, and scientists have found that its balance shifts during spaceflight.
Most knowledge about astronaut health comes from small crews living aboard the ISS for months at a time, which is why a study of 52 astronauts counts as a large sample in this field.

NASA's Artemis program (the effort to send people back to the Moon and eventually on to Mars) means crews will spend far longer in space than before, so a nuisance like constipation becomes a serious planning problem.

On Earth, products of protein fermentation are linked to the same kinds of harm seen in kidney disease and some digestive disorders, so researchers think space research could end up helping patients at home.

perspectives.description: Knowing that protein fermentation is behind astronaut constipation suggests concrete fixes such as fiber, prebiotics or drugs that boost peristalsis, which could protect crews on long missions.

The study followed only 52 astronauts and found associations in blood, not proof of cause; spaceflight also changes diet, sleep, stress and radiation exposure, so pinning the effect on microgravity alone is difficult.

Protein fermentation already happens in human guts on Earth when fiber is scarce; space simply seems to push an existing mechanism further, which makes the finding less a new phenomenon than a change in degree.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — from orbit to the clinic
perspectives.description: If researchers can confirm the mechanism, the same treatments might be tested on Earth for people whose gut bacteria over-ferment protein, turning a space-health study into broader medical knowledge.
